beats.note: It appears for the first time in Karel Capek's R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots), published in 1920 and staged in Prague in 1921. Before that, the word did not exist.

beats.lead: It was never a word for 'machine'
beats.note: From the Czech 'robota': the unpaid drudgery a serf owed his lord. The deeper Slavic root, 'rab', means slave. The name was built to mean bondage.

beats.lead: And the first robots weren't metal
beats.note: Rossum's robots are not clanking machines but mass-produced living workers, grown rather than built, far closer to lab-made humans than to anything with gears.

beats.text: The robots rise and end humanity.
beats.note: The very first tale to use the word is also the first robot uprising. By the final act, mankind is gone. The trope arrived fully formed, a century ago.

beats.text: Our word for machines was coined for slaves made of flesh.

beats.line: A hundred years on, we still borrow their name.
